From Chhatrapati Shivaji terminus to the ‘White town’ to the University library to the magnificent Marine drive, the city has so many spectacular attractions that one can never miss. Explore all these places of Old Mumbai and many more with this heritage walk tour.

Walking tours expose many residents and visitors to the structures.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Rajabai Tower, University of Mumbai: The Mumbai University is undoubtedly one of the finest examples of Victorian Neo Gothic
Architecture in Mumbai. It is also an integral part of one of the finest urban ensembles of Victorian buildings in the world. The Rajabai Tower, with its imposing skyline, dominates the skyline of the Fort area, thus further strengthening its classification for reasons of scenic value.
The Mumbai University, designed by Sir Gilbert Scott, is an example of a public project in the city funded by local philanthropists, in this case, the "Cotton King" of Bombay, Premchund Roychund who made a generous contribution of Rupees 4 lakhs towards its construction. As a gesture of acknowledgment, the lofty Rajabai Tower, an awesome structure that rose to a height of 260 feet, was named after his mother. The Library structure adjoining the Rajabai Tower has among the finest ensembles of stained glass in the country while the splendid cross vaulted roof of the Reading Room with its polished timber members, is among the most spectacular architectural interiors in the city.

Built in 1878, it stands as a historical landmark and one of Mumbai's iconic structures. The 85-meter-tall tower is adorned with exquisite stained glass windows and intricate carvings, making it a treat for architecture enthusiasts. Named after Rajabai, the mother of its patron, Premchand Roychand, the tower is not only a testament to Mumbai's colonial heritage but also a functioning clock tower. It offers picturesque views and is a must-visit for history lovers and tourists exploring the city's cultural landmarks.

featured_reviews.name: Rahul
featured_reviews.review_text:
Beautiful place which is seen from city
The 142-year-old Rajabai Clock Tower in South Mumbai’s Fort area, located inside University of Mumbai’s campus, is iconic for its Victorian-Gothic architecture. Built in 1878 by architect Sir George Gilbert Scott, it was commissioned by businessman Premchand Roychand as a tribute to his mother, hence the name. For years, it was the city’s tallest structure, at 285 feet. Rajabai Clock Tower has long been a beacon of the Oval Maidan precinct, a visual delight, and a valuable piece of history for the city. After brilliant restoration work by SNK Consultants, the clock tower was handed over to KSA Lighting Designers in 2017 for lighting the tower, the facade and the interiors of the University Library. Kanchan Puri, principal at the firm, tells us the process of this massive undertaking that was completed recently. After years of darkness, the Rajabai Clock Tower finally glowed up in 2021, literally.

🚉 Must-visit experience in Mumbai — seriously, don’t miss this!

If you think you know Mumbai, think again. The “Crown Jewel of Mumbai” Heritage Tour at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) is an absolute show-stopper. For just ₹500 on BookMyShow (and yes, no walk-ins — exclusivity adds to the thrill 😉), this guided tour unlocks parts of CSMT most Mumbaikars have only rushed past while chasing trains.

The journey takes you through the Heritage Gallery, Railway Museum, Central Dome, and the stunning Star Chamber — and trust me, this is one train you’ll want to slow down for. You’ll uncover jaw-dropping British-era history, architectural secrets hidden in plain sight, and UNESCO heritage spaces that finally make you stop, stare, and look up (literally and emotionally).

And the cherry on this heritage cake? Our guide, Ian. Knowledgeable, patient, and effortlessly engaging, he brought the stones, stories, and structures to life — from intricate Gothic architecture to fascinating railway history. Not a single dull moment; every explanation felt like a plot twist.

If you’ve ever walked through CSMT thinking “one day I’ll explore this properly,” this is your sign. Miss this tour, and you’ll definitely suffer from heritage FOMO. 🚆✨

featured_reviews.review_text:

We often travel or visit distant places to see historic architecture, but having something this magnificent right in Mumbai is really special. These details usually go unnoticed, but once you start observing, the beauty becomes very evident.

The museum hosts a railway heritage exhibition, spread across the ground and first floor. Entry is through online slot booking, and the entry fee is around ₹500. When I checked, the available time slots were after 4 PM, and since I had other plans, I couldn’t book a slot.

Even without entering the museum, just viewing the building from the outside was a wonderful experience.

featured_reviews.name: Gopal Pandia
featured_reviews.review_text:
Standing proudly beside the Arabian Sea, the Gateway of India is one of the most iconic landmarks in Mumbai and a place that truly captures the spirit of the city. The grand architecture, inspired by Indo-Saracenic style, looks even more beautiful in real life than in pictures. The detailed design, huge arch, and historical importance make this place a must-visit for every traveller.

The atmosphere around the monument is always lively. You can see tourists taking photos, local people enjoying the sea breeze, street vendors selling snacks, and ferries moving across the water towards Elephanta Caves. Early morning and evening are the best times to visit because the weather feels pleasant and the view during sunset is absolutely stunning.

One of the best parts about visiting here is the location itself. Right beside the Gateway stands the famous Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, which adds even more charm to the area. The entire surroundings feel energetic and full of history. Security arrangements are good, and the area is mostly clean despite being crowded.

The place can get very busy during weekends and holidays, so visiting on a weekday is a better option if you want to enjoy peacefully. Parking nearby can be difficult, and local taxi or cab services are usually more convenient. There are many food stalls and cafés around where visitors can enjoy Mumbai’s famous snacks after exploring the monument.

Overall, the Gateway of India is not just a tourist spot, it is an experience that reflects the culture, history, and beauty of Mumbai. A perfect place for photography, sightseeing, and spending quality time with family or friends. Definitely worth visiting at least once.

featured_reviews.name: Shubham Prince
featured_reviews.review_text:
I visited Gateway of India mainly to head to Elephanta Caves and honestly, this is where you need to be careful.
Many ticket sellers will confidently tell you the ticket is for Elephanta Caves, but in reality, some of them are just round-trip joy rides that bring you back to the Gateway itself.
Important note:
If you’re actually going to Elephanta Caves, make sure:
1. You go before 3 PM
2. The ticket price is around ₹130 or more Cheaper tickets are usually not for the caves — learned this the hard way.
The place is extremely crowded, the heat can be brutal, and you’ll need patience. The vibe is energetic though, street noise, tourists everywhere, boats lining up, and the iconic view of the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel right in front of you.
Plenty of photographers will approach you. If you do get photos clicked, ask for digital copies. The printed versions are honestly poor in quality and not worth it.
Overall experience?
The enthusiasm is there, the atmosphere is lively, but it does feel a bit overhyped. Not bad, not amazing  just… fine.
Still, it’s one of those places you experience once, observe everything, question a few things internally, and move on.
Enjoy your time at the Gateway — just go informed.

Historical landmark and UNESCO world heritage place as well.
Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) is the true crown jewel of Mumbai's public infrastructure. Walking into this UNESCO World Heritage site feels like stepping into a living history museum. Functionally, it serves as the massive beating heart of Central Railway, managing millions of local and long-distance passengers daily with stellar efficiency. Navigating the station during peak rush hour can be intense, but the layout is grand and iconic. It is a must-visit landmark for history buffs and daily commuters alike

Even before entering the station, the grand Gothic-style architecture immediately caught my attention. The detailed carvings, domes, arches, and stained-glass windows make the building look more like a historic monument than a railway station.
Inside, the atmosphere is lively and intense, with thousands of people moving in different directions. Despite the constant rush, I found it fascinating how smoothly everything functions. Watching the trains arrive and depart while standing inside such a magnificent heritage structure felt surreal. It is a place where history and everyday life blend seamlessly.
What impressed me most was how CSMT represents the spirit of Mumbai. There is chaos, energy, discipline, and resilience all at once. The station tells stories of the city’s colonial past while continuing to serve as a lifeline for millions of commuters every day. Taking a moment to pause and observe people from different walks of life added depth to the visit.
Overall, CSMT is not just a transit point but an experience in itself. It left me with a deeper appreciation for Mumbai’s history, architecture, and unstoppable rhythm of life.

Recently, I visited Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, and it was a truly memorable experience. Even though it is one of the busiest railway stations in India, the first thing that caught my attention was its incredible architecture. The building is a perfect blend of Victorian Gothic and Indian architectural styles, making it look more like a grand historical monument than a railway station.

As soon as I arrived, I was amazed by the detailed carvings, large domes, stained-glass windows, and the overall grandeur of the structure. It is easy to understand why this station is considered one of Mumbai's most important landmarks. During the evening, when the building is illuminated, it looks even more beautiful and provides excellent opportunities for photography.

Inside the station, there is a constant flow of passengers from different parts of the city and country. The atmosphere is energetic and reflects the fast-paced life of Mumbai. Despite the large crowds, the station is generally well-organized with clear signboards, ticket counters, waiting areas, and various food stalls.

What impressed me the most was how the station combines history with modern transportation. Every day, thousands of people pass through it, yet it still preserves its heritage and charm. Standing there, I felt connected to a piece of Mumbai's rich history while also witnessing the city's modern rhythm.

Of course, like any major railway station, it can become extremely crowded during peak hours, and finding a comfortable place to sit may sometimes be difficult. However, these minor inconveniences are overshadowed by the station's beauty, historical significance, and importance to daily life.

Overall, CSMT is much more than a railway station. It is a symbol of Mumbai's heritage, culture, and spirit. I would highly recommend visiting it, even if you are not traveling by train, just to experience its unique atmosphere and architectural magnificence.

From a functionality perspective, it’s extremely busy. Being one of the main hubs for local and long-distance trains, the crowds can get overwhelming, especially during peak hours. Navigation inside the station can be confusing for first-time visitors, but signage has improved over time.
Facilities like ticket counters, digital boards, and waiting areas are decent, though cleanliness varies depending on the time of day. Security is generally good, with constant police presence.
Connectivity is excellent—easy access to taxis, buses, and nearby areas like Fort and Crawford Market.

Overall, CSMT is not just a station—it’s an experience of Mumbai’s energy and heritage.

featured_reviews.name: sajid shaikh
featured_reviews.review_text:
This was my third Umrah trip with Rahat Tours, but sadly this time the experience was quite disappointing.

We had booked a silver package, however the hotel provided felt closer to a bronze standard and was located far from the Haram, which made it very exhausting to travel back and forth.

The overall management and staff support were not up to the mark. There seemed to be a lack of coordination and professionalism throughout the journey. When we arrived at the hotel in Madina, there was no assistance with luggage, which was unexpected and disappointing.

While returning to Makkah, we were told that the bus would arrive at 2:00 PM, but even by 5:00 PM there was no sign of it. Delays can happen, but the absence of proper communication reflects poorly on the management.

At one point, we asked different staff members about the hotel location in Makkah, and we received completely conflicting information. It was confusing and felt very unprofessional.

In comparison, during a previous Umrah trip with Bakhla Tours, the service was much better. The staff was cooperative and helpful, especially when it came to handling luggage and overall guidance.

Alhamdulillah, we were still able to complete our Umrah, but overall the experience did not meet expectations. I would recommend choosing well-established tour operators like Al Irfan or Atlas, as better management can make a big difference in such a spiritual journey.

I hope this feedback is taken positively and improvements are made in staff behavior, communication, and overall service for future pilgrims.

featured_reviews.name: Bella
featured_reviews.review_text:
As a solo female traveller, I was happy with my experience staying here. I booked a private room for a reasonable price, which came with A/C and a balcony. The room was clean, functional, and comfortable enough for a simple stay. The building has a heritage feel, so expect older features like peeling wood and some cracks. Shared washrooms are basic. Soundproofing is limited, so bring earplugs.

This place is best suited for solo travellers looking for a practical base rather than a social or tourist vibe. Most guests are domestic (and men), either in transit or travelling for work, so people keep to themselves.

Staff are helpful when asked but don’t offer things automatically. If you need amenities like a door lock, towels, or toilet paper, you’ll need to request them and there may be a small charge.

They also stored my luggage for free, which was convenient.

Bring cash if possible, as card payments incur a 6 percent fee. But the owner is happy for you to pay later so you can withdraw cash nearby and avoid the fee.

There's a dedicated jogging path which offers you a soft landing.. ideal for jogging... There are several exercise machine too which help you exercise without going to expensive gyms... Also offering the serene and lush green environment which is so recommended for exercise and workout.

Once you've sweated it out, you can relax and cool down on the several swings that are installed all around the park. Yoga enthusiasts have a dedicated area which is cemented and has a concrete canopy offering you a really cool and breezy surrounding to get relaxed with yogic exercises and postures. The huge Banyan trees in the central area of the park provide a thicket of cool space where you can relax, read your favourite book, listen to music or discourses or even hear a narrated story on your smart device.

The small and artificial lake provides soothing comfort(though the water is in need of treatment and regular circulation). The bridge over the lake too is a picturesque sight.

In all, its truly a place to exercise your body and compose your mind.
I came back energized and yet calm.. Do take out time and visit... You won't regret it.

featured_reviews.review_text:
### **Gilbert Hill: A 66-Million-Year-Old Oasis Above the Urban Chaos**
**Rating: ★★★★☆**
A visit to Gilbert Hill is a surreal Mumbai experience that feels like stepping back in time while standing in the middle of a modern metropolis. As one of only three volcanic basalt monoliths of its kind in the world, the sheer geological significance of this 200-foot rock is staggering.
**The Experience:**
The climb involves about 200 steep steps, which takes roughly 15 minutes. At the summit, the **Gaondevi** and **Durga Devi** temples offer a surprisingly tranquil atmosphere that feels worlds away from the city's noise. The 360-degree view is the real highlight—a startling juxtaposition where glitzy high-rises sit directly alongside sprawling slum clusters, providing a raw, unfiltered look at Mumbai’s social fabric.
**Crucial Logistic Warning:**
Do **not** attempt to drive a large SUV or private vehicle to the base. The "roads" leading here are extremely narrow, congested lanes through dense residential pockets. Navigating a big vehicle is a nightmare, and parking is non-existent.
**Pro-Tip:**
Take a rickshaw from Andheri Station or park your car in a commercial lot in Andheri West and walk the last stretch. It’s a hidden gem that rewards the effort, just leave the heavy wheels behind!

featured_reviews.name: Deuba Sarkar
featured_reviews.review_text: Gilbert Hill is a 200 ft (61 m) monolith column of black basalt rock at Andheri, in Mumbai, India. The rock has a sheer vertical face and was formed when molten lava was squeezed out of the Earth's clefts during the Mesozoic Era about 66 million years ago. During that era, molten lava had spread around most of the Indian states of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, covering an area of 50,000 square kilometres (19,000 sq mi). The volcanic eruptions were also responsible for the destruction of plant and animal life during that era. According to experts, this rare geological phenomenon was the remnant of a ridge and had clusters of vertical columns in nearby Jogeshwari which were quarried off two decades ago.These vertical columns are similar to the Devils Tower National Monument in Wyoming, and the Devils Postpile National Monument in eastern California, USA. Gilbert Hill was declared a National Park in 1952 by the Central Government under the Forest Act. In 2007, after years of lobbying by geologists, the hill was declared a Grade II heritage structure by the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM), and all quarrying and other activities around the monument were prohibited. Over the period of time,Gilbert Hill has faced severe erosion problems too
